docs.title: ncCore Documentation
docs.text:
ncCore is a grblHAL motion controller built for one job: replacing the controller in a CNC you already own without rewiring the machine. One mainboard carries the motion, I/O, power and safety circuits. A small adapter card per machine presents the connectors your machine's harness already uses, so a conversion is unplug, plug in, flash. It is made for ncSender.

Preliminary documentation

ncCore is in its prototype stage. Everything here describes the design as drawn. Pin orders marked provisional have not yet been confirmed on a real machine, and specifications will be re-measured on production hardware. Treat this manual as a working draft until the first boards ship.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Does ncCore have stepper drivers? No, by design. It drives external drivers, and it is aimed at closed-loop motors with the driver built in. Onefinity Elite and Redline and AltMill motors are all like that. For a Shapeoko or a machine with open-loop motors on the old controller board, you need drivers or new motors.

Which machines have adapters? Onefinity Elite and Redline, AltMill, and a DIY terminal card. See Machine Adapters.

Can I use it without an adapter card? Yes. The 64-pin header and the XT30 are documented, and the DIY card puts everything on screw terminals.

Is the E-stop real? Yes. It is a hardware loop that removes motor power and the spindle enable with no firmware involved. See Emergency Stop.

What power supply do I need? 24 to 48 V DC. Usually the one your machine already has.

Does it work with the ncSender pendant? Yes, unchanged. The pendant pairs with its own dongle on the computer running ncSender.

What is ncBridge? A wireless I/O module that talks to ncCore's radio, for inputs and outputs on moving parts of the machine. See ncSender & ncBridge.

Can I run it from a Raspberry Pi kiosk? Yes. ncSender runs on a Pi, and ncCore connects to it over USB or Wi-Fi.

Is the firmware open? Yes. It is upstream grblHAL with an open board map.

Where are the design files? The hardware design is not public. The grblHAL board map and firmware will be published once the first boards ship.

docs.title: Board
docs.text:
Outline 145 × 93 mm Mounting holes Four, M3 clearance, one per corner, isolated from both grounds Hole positions 12 mm in from the left edge, 5.5 mm in from the right edge, 5.5 mm in from the top and bottom edges Tallest parts The input inductor, the bulk capacitors and the Mini-Fit power connector, all under 15 mm

The adapter header and XT30 are on the left edge; the adapter card stacks there on the ribbon. Leave room on the left for the ribbon's bend and the card.

docs.title: Adapter cards
docs.text: All adapters share one outline, about 92.5 × 57.5 mm, with the header and XT30 at the same positions, so any card fits the same enclosure end wall. The machine-side connectors stand vertically on the outer face; the header and XT30 are on the inner face.

docs.title: Bare board in a panel
docs.text: Mount on standoffs on a back plate. The four holes are isolated, so a grounded plate is fine. Bring the ribbon and the XT30 lead to your own breakout, or to a DIY adapter mounted beside the board. Keep the VFD and its motor cable on the far side of the panel from the ribbon.

docs.title: Minimal enclosure
docs.text:
The optional enclosure is a two-part box. The mainboard sits in the base, the adapter card stands as the end wall so the machine's plugs face out, and the other end is cut for the panel terminal, the two USB ports and the antenna. It is sold separately.

For a metal enclosure, use the U.FL antenna connector with an external antenna rather than the chip antenna; the antenna select is a solder link next to the radio.

docs.title: Nothing lights, or only REVERSED lights
docs.text: The supply is connected backwards. The ideal diode blocked it and nothing was harmed. Swap the wires at the power connector.

docs.title: ENABLED never lights
docs.text: The E-stop loop is open. Check that the mushroom is released, that OUT and RET on the panel terminal are wired through a normally-closed contact, and that any door switches in the loop are closed. With no E-stop wired at all, the loop is open by design; fit the BYPASS jumper only if your machine's own E-stop cuts the supply.

docs.title: Motors do not enable
docs.text:
• Check $4, the enable invert.
  • Onefinity Elite motors need 5 V or more on ENA+. If they refuse, tie ENA+ to the fused 5 V on the adapter; see the Elite adapter.
  • The motor bus is off while the E-stop loop is open. Check ENABLED.

docs.title: An axis alarms immediately
docs.text: The alarm input polarity is wrong for your driver. Open-collector alarms are low when healthy and need the input inverted. A disconnected alarm wire on such a driver also reads as an alarm, which is the fail-safe behaviour.

docs.title: A limit shows triggered all the time
docs.text:
• Normally-closed sensor: invert the input with $5.
  • Wrong COM setting for the sensor type: see Limits & Homing.
  • Wrong sensor supply: an inductive sensor rated 10 to 30 V will not switch on 5 V. Move LIMIT V.

The LED beside the input shows the raw electrical state and helps tell wiring from settings.

docs.title: The spindle runs but the speed is wrong
docs.text: $30 sets the rpm that corresponds to 10 V. Match it to the VFD's maximum frequency setting. If the VFD reads the analog input against its own common, make sure that common is wired to GND.

docs.title: Modbus VFD does not respond
docs.text: Check A and B are not swapped, the VFD's Modbus address, baud rate and parity match the plugin settings, and the RS485 TERM jumper is fitted. The 485 TX LED blinks when ncCore transmits; RX blinks when the VFD answers.

docs.title: ncSender loses the connection when E-stop is pressed
docs.text: On machines whose E-stop cuts the supply, the board stays up on USB power if the USB cable is connected. Over Wi-Fi alone, the radio loses power with the supply. Use USB, or keep the machine supply on and use ncCore's own E-stop loop.

docs.title: A firmware update failed
docs.text: Use the recovery procedure in Flashing & Recovery. The ROM bootloaders on both chips cannot be erased.

docs.title: How Adapters Work
docs.text:
The mainboard is the same for every machine. What changes is a small passive card that presents your machine's own connectors, so the stock cables plug straight in.

flowchart LR
  MB[ncCore mainboard] -- 64-way ribbon --> AD[Adapter card]
  MB -- XT30 motor bus --> AD
  AD --> M1[Motor connectors]
  AD --> S1[Homing sensors]
  AD --> P1[Probe, tool setter]
  AD --> V1[Spindle / VFD]
  AD --> C1[Coolant]

An adapter card carries no logic. It fans the 64 header pins and the motor bus out to connectors, ties a few pins where a machine needs a fixed level, and carries the motor current on wide copper. In the minimal enclosure it stands as the end wall, so every machine plug faces out.

docs.title: What an adapter decides
docs.text:
Motor bus XT30 on every adapter
  • Which connector family: the same Molex, JST or pluggable-terminal families as the original controller.
  • Pin order inside each plug, matched to the machine's cables.
  • How the enable is presented: as a differential pair, or single-ended against ground.
  • How the alarm is presented: an opto pair, or the alarm line against a fixed 5 V.
  • What the sensors are fed: the fused 5 V or 24 V from the header.
  • Extras the original controller lacked, such as an RS-485 port for Modbus or coolant outputs.

docs.title: AltMill Adapter
docs.text:
For the Sienci AltMill, which ships with the SuperLongBoard EXT and the SLB-EXT harness. The adapter carries the SLB-EXT connector families, so the stock cables plug straight in.

Status

Designed from Sienci's published SLB-EXT pinout. The motor ribbon's physical pin order is reported inconsistently between the published schematic and the pin list; confirm it on a real ribbon before relying on it.

An AltMill conversion is a lateral move on firmware, since the SLB is already grblHAL. What ncCore adds is the ncSender integration, the wireless I/O, and the mainboard's own aux I/O and outputs.

docs.title: DIY & Other Machines
docs.text: For a scratch build, or a machine nobody has made an adapter for yet, the DIY adapter brings every header signal to a screw terminal, and the motor bus to a pair of heavy terminals.

docs.title: Two ways to wire a custom machine
docs.text:
With the DIY terminal adapter. Every one of the 64 header pins lands on a labelled screw terminal, grouped by axis and function, plus the motor bus. Wire your drivers, sensors and VFD to the terminals following the I/O Reference.

With your own panel. If you already have a cabinet with contactors, relays, solenoids and a VFD on one back plate, run the 64-way ribbon from the mainboard's header into your panel and land it on your own breakout, and bring the motor bus in on the XT30. The Adapter Header page has the pinout; the Motors page has the enable and alarm rules that matter most.

docs.title: The rules that catch people
docs.text:
• Never ground ENA_N. Use ENA_P against GND for a single-ended enable and leave ENA_N open.
  • Alarm inputs are bare opto LEDs. For an open-collector alarm, tie the alarm + to the fused 5 V and the alarm − to the driver's alarm pin.
  • Limits share one supply and one COM. Mixed NPN and PNP sensors on the limit bank do not work; use the aux inputs' second bank for the odd one out.
  • The header's fused rails are for sensors, 1.1 A each. Power a VFD's control side or a relay coil from the aux outputs or your own supply.
  • The motor bus is switched by the E-stop. Your drivers lose power when the loop opens. That is the point. If your drivers need standby power to keep position, wire the E-stop to your driver's own enable instead and fit the BYPASS jumper, but then ncCore is no longer the thing stopping the machine.

docs.title: Making a real adapter
docs.text: The three existing adapters share one outline, with the header and XT30 in the same place, so a new one fits the enclosure. Copy one in the design files, change the connectors, and route it. The Masso adapter is the most recent and is a good template for a machine that carries motor power in the signal cable.

docs.title: Onefinity Elite (Masso) Adapter
docs.text:
For the Onefinity Gen 1 Elite series, Foreman, Journeyman, Woodworker and Machinist, which ship with the MASSO G3 Touch controller. The adapter carries the same Molex families as the Elite's controller box and adds a GX12 spindle socket.

Provisional pin order

Onefinity publishes the connector families and the wire colours but not the cavity order inside each plug, and lists the motor plug as 8, 10 or 12 circuits without saying which. Every cavity assignment on this page is a working assumption to be confirmed on a real Elite controller before the adapter is produced. If you have an Elite and a multimeter, a buzz-out of one motor plug, one homing plug and the GX12 would settle it.

docs.title: The Elite motor cable
docs.text:
Motor connector, Mini-Fit Jr 2×4, header face. Provisional

The Elite's motors are MASSO closed-loop steppers with the driver inside, model HT-SCL-1.2NM, 36 V, 4.5 A. Their eight wires:

Motor terminal Wire Adapter net 36VDC red Motor bus GND black GND S+ / S− yellow / orange Axis step ± D+ / D− gray / black Axis direction ± ENA+ green ENA_P ALM+ purple Axis alarm −, with alarm + tied to the fused 5 V

There is no ENA− or ALM− on these motors; both are referenced to motor ground. The MASSO drives step and direction differentially, exactly as ncCore does.

Enable: the motor wants 5 to 24 V to enable. On the factory Elite it is wired to the E-stop output, so the motors are enabled whenever the E-stop is released. The adapter uses ENA_P, which lets grblHAL disable the motors, but an RS-422 high is around 3.8 V and may sit under the motor's threshold. If the motors do not enable, the fallback is to tie ENA+ to the fused 5 V on the adapter, which reproduces the factory behaviour.

Alarm: ALM+ is an open collector, low when healthy. Invert the alarm inputs in grblHAL.

docs.title: Flashing & Recovery
docs.text: ncCore has two chips and two USB-C ports. The STM32 runs grblHAL and talks to ncSender on the port marked USB. The ESP32-S3 runs the radio firmware and has its own port marked RADIO USB. Both ports sit on the isolated logic side, and either one also powers the logic side, so you can flash with no machine power connected.

docs.title: Updating grblHAL
docs.text: The normal path is ncSender. Connect on the USB port, open Settings, Firmware, and pick the release. ncSender sends the board into DFU mode with $DFU, flashes the image, and reconnects. Nothing on the board needs pressing.

docs.title: Recovering the STM32
docs.text:
If the firmware is corrupt or the chip is blank and does not answer $DFU:

  1. Hold BOOT on the mainboard.
  2. Press and release RESET, or plug the USB cable in while holding BOOT.
  3. Release BOOT. The chip is now in its ROM DFU mode, which cannot be erased or bricked.
  4. Flash from ncSender's firmware page, which recognises a DFU device, or with STM32CubeProgrammer.

On Windows, ST's ROM DFU carries no driver descriptors, so the device may show without a driver until STM32CubeProgrammer or a WinUSB driver is installed. A future firmware release will let the ESP32 flash the STM32 over its own port to avoid this; the hardware for it is on the board.

A blank chip straight from the factory can also be programmed through the five-pin SWD header, 3V3, DIO, CLK, RST, GND, with an ST-Link.

docs.title: Updating the radio
docs.text:
The ESP32-S3 firmware is updated from ncSender's accessories page over Wi-Fi. If the radio is unresponsive:

  1. Hold PAIR / BOOT.
  2. Plug a USB cable into RADIO USB, or press the ESP32's reset if fitted, then release the button.
  3. The chip is in its ROM download mode. Flash with the ncSender web flasher or esptool.

ncSender can stay connected on the USB port throughout.

docs.title: Antenna and radio
docs.text: The radio uses the chip antenna by default. For a metal enclosure, move the solder link near the radio to the U.FL position and fit an external antenna. Only one of the two may be selected.

docs.title: grblHAL on ncCore
docs.text: ncCore runs upstream grblHAL on its STM32F407, with a board map that describes where every signal is. The board map, nccore_map.h, will be published with the firmware once the first boards ship.

docs.title: What the board map defines
docs.text:
Group Signals Axes X, Y, Z, A step and direction. Y1 and Y2 are grblHAL's Y and its ganged Y2, with separate step, direction and alarm Enable One shared enable output Alarms Five motor-fault inputs, one per axis Limits X, X2, Y, Y2, Z, A Probe and tool setter Two dedicated inputs Controls Door, feed hold, cycle start, reset Aux inputs Eight, exposed through ioports Aux outputs Four, plus flood and mist, exposed through ioports Spindle PWM, enable, direction; the 0–10 V follows the PWM RS-485 USART1, for the Modbus VFD plugin Radio USART3 to the ESP32-S3, plus four fast lines for the wireless probe and tool setter Status ENABLED, RUN and FAULT LEDs; the E-stop loop and motor-bus monitors

The pin assignments were laid out by package side, so each group of pins faces the circuit it drives.

docs.title: Firmware-side safety rules
docs.text:
The hardware makes some behaviour mandatory in firmware:

  • A motor-bus fault, the loop open while the bus reads live, must raise an alarm and refuse motion.
  • Loss of the machine supply, bus-OK low while running on USB, must require homing before the next move.
  • A wireless input whose link is lost must be invalidated and raise an alarm. E-stop, limits and door never go over the wireless link.

docs.title: Building
docs.text: The map targets the grblHAL STM32F4xx driver. Add nccore_map.h to the driver's boards folder, add a BOARD_NCSENDER_NCCORE case to the board selection, and build with the axis count you need, up to four axes plus ganged Y. Pre-built images will be published with each release, and ncSender flashes them for you; see Flashing & Recovery.

docs.title: Plugins that matter on this board
docs.text: Plugin Why Spindle VFD (Modbus) Huanyang, Delta and generic profiles for the RS-485 port Virtual inputs Wireless probe, tool setter and aux inputs from an ncBridge Motor fault handling Maps the alarm inputs to alarms with position intact

docs.title: Connecting ncSender
docs.text:
Path How USB A USB-C cable to the port marked USB. ncSender finds the board as a serial port Wi-Fi The ESP32-S3 joins your network and ncSender connects to it. Set up the radio once from ncSender's accessories page over USB

ncSender's First Connection and Machine Setup Wizard pages cover the software side. The wizard tests axis direction, homing and the inputs, and writes the settings.

docs.title: The pendant
docs.text: The ncSender wireless pendant works with ncCore exactly as with any other controller: it pairs with its dongle on the computer running ncSender. Nothing about the pendant changes.

docs.title: ncBridge
docs.text:
ncBridge is a wireless I/O module for the parts of the machine a wire cannot reach: the moving gantry, a rotary table, a dust boot. It has its own power input, four selectable-voltage outputs, four opto-isolated inputs and an LED strip port, and it talks to ncCore's ESP32-S3 over ESP-NOW.

On ncCore, an ncBridge input becomes a grblHAL aux input and an ncBridge output a grblHAL aux output, through the virtual-inputs plugin. A wireless probe or tool setter on an ncBridge triggers through the fast lines between the radio and the MCU, with no software in the path.

Pair an ncBridge by pressing PAIR / BOOT on the mainboard and the pairing button on the ncBridge. ncSender's accessories page shows the paired devices and their signal strength.

What never goes wireless

E-stop, limits and the door are wired inputs only. A lost radio link invalidates the wireless inputs and raises an alarm; it can never silently keep a machine running.

docs.title: Ganged Y
docs.text: If your machine has two Y motors, enable ganged axes and auto-squaring so grblHAL homes Y1 and Y2 to their own sensors and squares the gantry.

docs.title: Aux I/O
docs.text: Aux inputs and outputs need no settings; they appear in ncSender's I/O panel by number. Assign the tool setter and any plugin inputs in ncSender.

docs.title: Adapter Header
docs.text:
The adapter header is a 64-pin keyed box header, 2 × 32 on 2.54 mm, marked ADAPTER on the mainboard. A 64-way ribbon connects it pin-for-pin to the adapter card, or to your own panel. The motor bus travels separately on the XT30.

Pin 1 is the square pad at the top left of the header. Odd pins are on the top row, even pins below, and the key notch is on the odd-pin side. Every differential pair sits across one column, so the pairs stay together on the ribbon.

5V_X and 24V_X are the mainboard's 5 V and 24 V rails through their own 1.1 A PTC fuses, for sensors and small loads on the adapter side. GND is the field ground.

docs.title: Signal groups
docs.text:
Motion, columns 1 to 32. For each axis a step pair, a direction pair and an alarm pair. Enable is one pair shared by all five axes, on pins 3 and 4. See Motors.

Machine I/O, spread between the axes. Limit inputs each sit beside a fused 5 V pin so a sensor can be powered from the same column. Probe, tool setter, RS-485, the spindle lines and the coolant switches complete the set.

ENA − is a driven output

Pins 3 and 4 are the two halves of an RS-422 pair. Never tie ENA_N to ground on an adapter or panel: four paralleled driver outputs would be shorted whenever the enable is high. For a single-ended enable use ENA_P against GND and leave ENA_N unconnected. See Motors.

docs.title: Using the header without an adapter
docs.text: The DIY adapter brings every pin to screw terminals. If you build your own panel instead, use a keyed 64-way IDC ribbon and observe the polarity notes above. Keep the ribbon under a metre, and keep it away from the VFD cable.

docs.title: Aux Inputs
docs.text: Eight general-purpose inputs on the mainboard's screw terminals, for things like a drawbar sensor, air pressure switch, enclosure interlock, dust-boot position or a vacuum switch. They do not go through the adapter header.

docs.title: Terminals
docs.text:
AUX-IN terminal, one per input

AUX-IN1 to AUX-IN8 are three-position screw terminals along the bottom edge, marked −, S and +.

Position Function − Ground S The input signal + The bank's sensor supply, selectable

docs.title: Banks
docs.text:
The inputs are in two banks of four, each with its own sensor supply and COM selector, so you can run 24 V inductive sensors on one bank and 5 V logic on the other.

Bank Inputs Supply selector COM selector A AUX-IN1 to AUX-IN4 IN1-4 V IN1-4 COM B AUX-IN5 to AUX-IN8 IN5-8 V IN5-8 COM

Each supply is 5, 12 or 24 V through a 1.1 A PTC. COM selects V+ for NPN sensors and dry switches, G for PNP sensors. See Jumpers, Buttons & LEDs.

docs.title: In the firmware
docs.text:
Each aux input is available to grblHAL as an auxiliary input through the ioports API. ncSender's plugins use them by name: the AutoDustBoot plugin reads its position sensor from one, a manual tool changer can wait on a drawbar sensor, and macros can wait on any of them with M66.

Every aux input has a blue LED beside its terminal.

docs.title: Operator controls
docs.text: Door, feed hold, cycle start and reset are separate inputs on the panel terminal, not aux inputs. They are dry contacts with a 12 V wetting supply and no selector.

docs.title: Aux Outputs, Flood & Mist
docs.text: Four protected outputs on screw terminals for accessories, plus flood and mist on the adapter header.

docs.title: Aux outputs
docs.text:
AUX-OUT terminal, one per output

AUX-OUT1 to AUX-OUT4 are two-position screw terminals, marked + and −.

Position Function + The output's supply: 5, 12 or 24 V, chosen with the OUTn V selector, through a 1.1 A PTC − The switched low side

Wire the load between + and −. When the output is on, the low side is pulled to ground and current flows. This is a low-side switch: the load's supply is always present on +, and the output controls the return.

Each output is a self-protected MOSFET with current limiting, short-circuit auto-restart and thermal shutdown, plus a flyback diode from the switched pin back to that port's + supply. That diode is what lets you drive a solenoid valve, a relay coil or a small pump directly. For an inductive load, do not add an external diode in the wrong direction; the on-board one is already there.

Parameter Value Continuous current per output 1.1 A, set by the PTC Supply 5, 12 or 24 V per output Isolation Digital isolator between the MCU and the switch; the output stays off when the logic side is unpowered

Typical uses: dust boot actuator, air blast valve, work light, vacuum relay, coolant pump relay, a status beacon.

docs.title: Flood and mist
docs.text:
Flood and mist use the same output stage but leave the board on the adapter header as FLOOD_SW and MIST_SW, switched low sides. Their load supply is the header's fused 5 V, 5V_X, so the adapter card presents each as a two-pin port: 24V_X or 5V_X on one pin and the switched return on the other, depending on the card.

grblHAL drives them with M7 (mist), M8 (flood) and M9 (off).

docs.title: In the firmware
docs.text: The aux outputs are grblHAL auxiliary outputs. Control them from G-code with M62 to M65, from ncSender's macros and plugins, or from the DRO's output buttons. ncSender's AutoDustBoot plugin, for example, drives its actuator from one of them.

docs.title: E-Stop Panel & Door
docs.text: The seven-position screw terminal marked PANEL / E-STOP carries the E-stop loop, three operator buttons and a lamp supply. The pin order is the same as Sienci's SLB and SLB-EXT E-stop box, so an AltMill owner moves the seven wires of that box straight across.

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text:
PANEL / E-STOP terminal J44, as printed on the board Pin Silk Net Function 1 GND GND Ground for the buttons 2 RST RESETI_IN Button: reset. Short to GND 3 HLD HOLD_IN Button: feed hold. Short to GND 4 RUN START_IN Button: cycle start. Short to GND 5 LMP ESTOP_LED Lamp supply: 24 V through 1 kΩ, only while the motor bus is live 6 RET ESTOP_OK E-stop loop return 7 OUT ESTOP_P E-stop loop out: 5 V through a PTC

The three buttons are dry contacts to GND. They have a 12 V wetting supply on the board and need no jumper. What each button does is a grblHAL assignment; reset, hold and start is the default mapping and matches Sienci's labels.

docs.title: Wiring the loop
docs.text:
Connect the mushroom's normally-closed contact between OUT and RET. Anything else you want in the chain, enclosure door switches, a second mushroom, a key switch, goes in series in the same loop.

OUT (7) ──[ NC mushroom ]──[ NC door switch ]── RET (6)

An open loop stops the motor bus and the spindle in hardware. See Emergency Stop.

docs.title: The lamp
docs.text: Pin 5 gives a lamp in the E-stop box a 24 V supply through 1 kΩ while the motor bus is live, so an illuminated button shows "enabled". It is a small-current supply for an LED lamp, not for an incandescent bulb.

docs.title: Bypass jumper
docs.text: J36, E-STOP BYPASS, connects OUT to RET on the board. Fit it only on machines whose own E-stop removes the DC supply: Onefinity Elite and Redline, and cabinets with a Nova panel or similar. With it fitted, ncCore has no E-stop of its own.

docs.title: Door switch
docs.text:
DOOR terminal J45

The two-position terminal marked DOOR, with positions S and −, takes a safety-door switch as a dry contact to ground. When the door opens, grblHAL pauses the job and, depending on settings, stops the spindle; when it closes, the job resumes. ncSender's Safety Door feature builds on this.

The door input has a blue LED beside its terminal.

docs.title: Limits & Homing
docs.text: Six limit inputs travel down the adapter header: X, X2, Y, Y2, Z and A. X2 and Y2 are for a second sensor on a dual-drive axis. All six share one sensor supply and one COM selector.

docs.title: The input stage
docs.text: Every machine input on ncCore uses the same stage: two 750 Ω resistors into an AC-input optocoupler, with the collector pulled up on the logic side. It accepts 3.3 to 24 V, does not care which way the current flows, and survives a 48 V miswire.

docs.title: Sensor supply
docs.text: The LIMIT V selector sets what the limit sensors are fed with: 5, 12 or 24 V, through a 1.1 A PTC. This voltage appears as the sensor supply on the adapter connectors and as the V+ position of the COM selector.

docs.title: NPN or PNP
docs.text:
Set LIMIT COM for your sensor type:

NPN sinking sensorPNP sourcing sensorMechanical switch

Most inductive proximity sensors and all mechanical switches wired to ground.

  • LIMIT COM shunt on V+
  • Sensor brown to the sensor supply, blue to GND, black (output) to the limit input
  • The input's LED lights when the sensor pulls its output low

Sensors that switch their supply voltage onto the output.

  • LIMIT COM shunt on G
  • Sensor brown to the sensor supply, blue to GND, black (output) to the limit input
  • The input's LED lights when the sensor sources current into the input

A dry contact between the limit input and GND.

  • LIMIT COM shunt on V+
  • Use the normally-closed contact if the switch offers one, and invert the input in grblHAL, so a broken wire reads as triggered

docs.title: Homing
docs.text:
grblHAL homes each axis toward its sensor and backs off. Settings that matter:

Setting Meaning $22 Enable homing $23 Homing direction mask $5 Limit pin invert, one bit per axis $24, $25 Homing feed and seek rates $27 Pull-off distance $20, $21 Soft and hard limits

After homing the machine knows where it is. ncSender's Machine Setup Wizard walks through direction and homing tests.

docs.title: Status LEDs
docs.text: Each limit input has a blue LED in the array beside the adapter header: LIM X, LIM X2, LIM Y, LIM Y2, LIM Z, LIM A. The LED shows current through the input, so with a normally-closed sensor it is lit while the loop is intact. ncSender shows the interpreted state.

docs.title: Motors: Step, Dir, Enable, Alarm
docs.text: ncCore has no stepper drivers on board. It drives external drivers, which on a modern conversion means closed-loop steppers with the driver built into the motor, or separate closed-loop drivers. Five axes are provided: X, Y1, Y2, Z and A.

docs.title: Step and direction
docs.text:
Each axis has a differential step pair and a differential direction pair from an AM26C31 RS-422 line driver on the logic side. Differential signalling is what lets the pairs cross the isolation barrier without a ground reference, and it is what long motor cables in a noisy cabinet need.

Parameter Value Levels RS-422, 5 V driver, about ±3.5 V differential into a 100 Ω pair Drive Enough for an opto-input driver, 10 mA or more per input Step pulse Set in grblHAL, $0. 5 µs is a safe default for most drivers

Differential inputs (STEP+, STEP−, DIR+, DIR−): connect the pairs straight through. This is how the Onefinity Elite, Redline and AltMill motors are wired.

Single-ended 5 V inputs (PUL+, PUL−, DIR+, DIR−, common-anode style): connect STEP+ to PUL+ and STEP− to PUL−. The driver's opto sits across the pair, which works with a differential source. Do not tie the − side to ground.

docs.title: Enable
docs.text:
Enable is one pair shared by all axes, ENA_P and ENA_N on header pins 3 and 4, driven by four paralleled channels of an AM26C31 on the field side. It is field-referenced on purpose, because most integrated drivers take a single-ended enable against motor ground.

Driver expects Wire Differential enable pair (EN+, EN−) ENA_P to EN+, ENA_N to EN−, as the AltMill adapter does Single-ended enable against ground, 5 to 24 V logic ENA_P to the driver's enable, driver ground to GND, ENA_N unconnected Enable that must sit at 5 V permanently 5V_X to the driver's enable. The controller then cannot disable the motors, which is how the Onefinity Elite is wired from the factory

Never ground ENA −

ENA_N is a push-pull driver output. Tying it to ground shorts the driver whenever the enable is high.

Polarity is set in grblHAL with $4. Some drivers enable on a high, some on a low.

docs.title: Alarm inputs
docs.text:
Each axis has an alarm input, x_ALM_P and x_ALM_N, which is a bare optocoupler LED with a 750 Ω series resistor on the mainboard. About 5 mA flows at 5 V. Because it is a bare LED, it works with every kind of alarm output:

Driver alarm output Wire Opto pair (ALM+, ALM−) x_ALM_P to ALM+, x_ALM_N to ALM−, as the AltMill adapter does Open collector to ground, active when faulted x_ALM_P to 5V_X, x_ALM_N to the driver's ALM pin. The LED is on while the driver holds ALM low, and goes off on a fault or a broken wire. This is the Onefinity Redline and Elite scheme Driven 5 V logic x_ALM_P to the signal, x_ALM_N to GND

Invert the alarm inputs in grblHAL to suit. The Redline and Elite scheme is fail-safe: a cut wire reads as an alarm.

When an alarm input asserts, grblHAL raises a motor-fault alarm and halts with position intact. Fix the cause, unlock and home.

docs.title: Y1 and Y2
docs.text: Y1 and Y2 are two motors on the same axis with separate step, direction and alarm, and, if you fit a second Y limit sensor, separate homing. Enable auto-squaring in grblHAL and the gantry is squared on every home. If your machine has a single Y motor, leave Y2 unconnected.

docs.title: Cable length
docs.text: RS-422 is comfortable over ten metres and more. Keep step, direction and enable in one shielded cable per axis, ground the shield at the controller end only, and route it away from the VFD's motor cable.

docs.title: Probe & Tool Setter
docs.text: Two dedicated inputs travel down the adapter header, PROBE_IN and TLS_IN. They share a fixed 5 V supply through a 1.1 A PTC and a COM selector marked PROBE COM.

docs.title: Why 5 V
docs.text: A touch plate or a probe tip only needs to close a circuit. Five volts does that, and it keeps a shorted probe lead harmless to the tool and the workpiece. The supply is not selectable.

docs.title: Touch plate or bare probe
docs.text:
The simplest probe is a plate or a tip that closes the input to ground through the tool.

  • PROBE COM shunt on V+
  • Plate to PROBE_IN, clip to GND
  • The input's LED lights on contact

docs.title: Powered probe or tool setter
docs.text:
A 3D touch probe or a tool setter with a built-in switch or sensor output:

Output type PROBE COM Wiring NPN, normally open or normally closed V+ Supply to the fused 5 V, ground to GND, signal to the input PNP G Same wiring Dry contact V+ Contact between the input and GND

Most tool setters are normally open. Invert the input in grblHAL if yours is normally closed. Many powered probes need 12 or 24 V; if yours does, power it from an aux-input sensor supply or the fused 24 V and bring only its output to the probe input.

docs.title: Wireless probe and tool setter
docs.text: ncCore has two direct lines from the radio to the motion MCU for a wireless probe or tool setter paired with the ESP32-S3. When the radio receives the trigger packet it raises the line with no software in between. This is how a wireless probe on an ncBridge can trigger fast enough to be useful. It is inert until the firmware enables it.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Meaning $6 Probe pin invert Tool-setter input Assigned in grblHAL's ioports; ncSender's probing and tool-change features use both

See ncSender's probing documentation for the probing workflows themselves.

docs.title: Spindle & VFD
docs.text: Everything the VFD sees is on the field side and crosses the isolation barrier through isolators. All of it leaves on the adapter header; the adapter card presents it in your machine's connector.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Signal Header net What it is 0–10 V SPIN_10V Analog speed reference, from a filtered 5 V PWM and an op-amp on the 24 V rail, through 100 Ω PWM SPIN_PWM_OUT The 5 V PWM itself, through 100 Ω. For lasers and drivers that take PWM Enable SPIN_EN_OD Open-drain, protected low-side switch. Sinks the VFD's run input to common Direction SPIN_DIR_OD Open-drain, same stage. Sinks the VFD's reverse input RS-485 RS485_A, RS485_B Isolated Modbus RTU, with a termination jumper

The enable and direction outputs are open-drain. They pull to GND when asserted, which matches how a VFD's FWD and REV inputs expect a contact closure to its common. If a machine needs 5 V logic instead, its adapter card adds a pull-up.

Spindle lines die with the E-stop

The field side of the spindle isolator is powered by the returned E-stop loop. When the loop opens, PWM, enable and direction all go inactive in hardware and the 0–10 V falls to zero. See Emergency Stop.

docs.title: Analog, 0–10 V
docs.text:
The most common VFD setup. Three wires from the adapter's spindle port:

VFD terminal Connect to VI or AI1, the analog speed input 0–10 V ACM or GND, analog common GND FOR or FWD, run forward Enable REV, run reverse, if used Direction DCM or COM, digital common GND

The VFD's digital common lands on ncCore's field ground. That is normal and is how the Onefinity Elite wires its GX12 spindle port.

docs.title: RS-485 Modbus
docs.text:
With Modbus the VFD is controlled over two wires and reports back: actual rpm, load, and fault codes, which ncSender shows. Connect A to A and B to B, and ground to the VFD's RS-485 common if it has one. Fit the RS485 TERM jumper when ncCore is at the end of the bus, which with a single VFD it is.

grblHAL's VFD spindle plugin supports Huanyang, several Delta and Yalang models and a generic Modbus profile. See ncSender's VFD setup guide for the VFD-side parameters.

The 485 TX and 485 RX LEDs blink with traffic.

docs.title: PWM and lasers
docs.text: A laser driver or a PWM-controlled spindle takes SPIN_PWM_OUT and GND. The PWM is 5 V logic through 100 Ω, at the frequency set in grblHAL.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Meaning $30, $31 Maximum and minimum spindle rpm, which scale the 0–10 V $32 Laser mode $33 PWM frequency Spindle type Chosen in grblHAL: PWM, Modbus VFD, or both

All the jumpers, buttons and LEDs are described in Jumpers, Buttons & LEDs.

docs.title: Layout logic
docs.text: The adapter header and the motor bus are on the left because the adapter card stacks there. The aux I/O is on screw terminals along the bottom because those are wired by hand, one at a time. The operator-facing connectors, power in, USB, antenna, door and panel, are on the right so the enclosure's end wall can carry them. The radio sits at that corner with a copper-free zone under the chip antenna.

docs.title: Rail selectors
docs.text:
Several inputs and outputs let you choose 5, 12 or 24 V. Each selector is a 2×3 header with a single shunt. The three positions are marked on the silk.

Selector Chooses Default Fused by LIMIT V Sensor supply for the six limit inputs 24 V 1.1 A PTC IN1-4 V Sensor supply for aux inputs 1 to 4 24 V 1.1 A PTC IN5-8 V Sensor supply for aux inputs 5 to 8 24 V 1.1 A PTC OUT1 V … OUT4 V The + supply of each aux output 24 V 1.1 A PTC per output

Probe and tool setter run from a fixed 5 V with their own PTC. A touch plate never needs more, and 5 V keeps a shorted probe wire harmless.

Move the shunt with power off

The selector switches the supply of a whole bank. Changing it live can glitch a sensor.

docs.title: Common selectors
docs.text:
Each input bank has a three-pin COM selector that sets what the inputs' opto-LEDs return to. This is what makes the inputs work with either sensor type.

Shunt position COM connects to Use with 1–2, marked V+ The bank's sensor supply NPN (sinking) sensors, bare touch plates, switches to ground 2–3, marked G Ground PNP (sourcing) sensors, switches to the supply

Selectors: LIMIT COM, PROBE COM, IN1-4 COM, IN5-8 COM. The four operator controls, door, hold, start and reset, have no selector: they are dry contacts to ground on a 12 V wetting supply.

docs.title: Other jumpers
docs.text: Jumper Function RS485 TERM Fits a 120 Ω termination across the RS-485 pair. Fit it when ncCore is at the end of the bus, which is the usual case with one VFD E-STOP BYPASS Shorts the E-stop loop on the board. Only for machines with their own power-cutting E-stop. See Emergency Stop Antenna select Two solder-link positions near the radio: chip antenna (default) or the U.FL socket for a metal enclosure. Never both

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: Button Chip Press Hold at power-up RESET STM32 Resets the controller BOOT STM32 ROM DFU mode for recovery flashing over the USB port PAIR / BOOT ESP32-S3 Starts pairing with an ncBridge ROM download mode for recovery flashing over the RADIO USB port

docs.title: LEDs
docs.text:
LED Colour Means ENABLED Green The E-stop loop is closed and the motor bus is enabled RUN Green grblHAL is running a job FAULT Red grblHAL alarm REVERSED Red The power supply is connected backwards. Nothing else lights LIM X, X2, Y, Y2, Z, A Blue Current is flowing through that limit input PROBE, TLS Blue Current is flowing through that input AUX-IN1 … 8, DOOR Blue Current is flowing through that input 485 TX Green Data leaving on RS-485 485 RX Red Data arriving on RS-485

The input LEDs show the raw electrical state, not the firmware's interpretation. A normally-open sensor lights its LED when triggered. A normally-closed sensor lights its LED while the loop is intact and goes dark when triggered. ncSender shows the interpreted state, after the invert settings.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text:
ncCore splits a controller into three parts.

flowchart LR
  subgraph PC["ncSender"]
    S[Desktop, kiosk or browser]
  end
  subgraph MB["ncCore mainboard"]
    L[Logic domain<br/>STM32F407 · ESP32-S3<br/>USB-C ×2 · antenna]
    F[Field domain<br/>power · motion drivers<br/>inputs · outputs · spindle · E-stop]
    L <-- isolators --> F
  end
  subgraph AD["Adapter card"]
    C[Your machine's own connectors]
  end
  S <-- USB or Wi-Fi --> L
  F <-- 64-way ribbon + XT30 --> C
  C --> M[Motors, sensors, spindle]
  B[ncBridge wireless I/O] <-. ESP-NOW .-> L

The mainboard is the same for every machine. It carries the STM32F407 running grblHAL, the ESP32-S3 radio, the power input and rails, the switched motor bus, five axes of differential step and direction, the alarm, limit, probe, control and aux inputs, the protected outputs, the spindle interface and the E-stop chain.

The adapter card is passive copper. It takes the mainboard's 64-pin header and the XT30 motor bus and fans them out to the connector families your machine's harness already uses. Each supported machine has its own card. A DIY card brings every signal to screw terminals.

ncSender is the sender, running on a PC, a kiosk or a tablet browser, over USB or Wi-Fi.

docs.text:

The two never share a ground. See Isolation & Grounding.

docs.title: Power path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  PSU[24–48 V DC] --> RP[Reverse protection<br/>ideal diode] --> FUSE[5 A fuse]
  FUSE --> BUS[Motor-bus switch<br/>E-stop controlled] --> XT[XT30 to adapter]
  FUSE --> B24[100 V buck] --> R24[24 V]
  R24 --> R12[12 V]
  R24 --> R5[5 V]
  R5 --> ISO[Isolated DC-DC] --> R5D[5 V logic] --> R33[3.3 V logic]
  USB[USB-C VBUS] --> R5D

The motor bus takes the raw input, current-limited and switched by the E-stop. The 24 V rail feeds sensors, aux outputs and the lower rails. The logic side has its own isolated supply and can also run from USB alone, so the controller stays up and reachable when the machine's supply is cut.

docs.title: Axes
docs.text: Five axes: X, Y1, Y2, Z and A. Y1 and Y2 are the two motors of a dual-drive gantry, each with its own step, direction and alarm, so grblHAL can auto-square the gantry. A is the rotary or a fifth linear axis.

docs.title: Motor Bus
docs.text: The motor bus is the raw input supply, switched and current-limited on the board and delivered to the adapter card through the XT30 socket marked MOTOR PWR.

docs.title: How it is switched
docs.text:
An LM5069 hot-swap controller drives a 100 V MOSFET in the bus. Its enable input is the returned E-stop loop, so:

  • Loop closed: after about 80 ms of debounce the FET soft-starts, limiting inrush into the drivers' capacitors.
  • Loop open: the FET turns off in microseconds.

There is no relay and no firmware in this path. See Emergency Stop.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Parameter Value Current limit About 18 A, set by a 3 mΩ sense resistor Over-voltage lockout About 57 V Connector XT30, rated 15 A continuous, 30 A burst

The current limit is a protection, not a rating. Sustained current near it will trip the controller's power-limit timer. For a machine with five 4.5 A closed-loop motors, plan on the supply and the input fuse, not the bus limit, being the constraint.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: The firmware reads MBUS_OK, an opto that is lit while the bus is live. A MOSFET can fail shorted, and if the E-stop loop is open while the bus still reads live, the firmware raises an alarm and refuses to run. ncSender shows this as a motor-bus fault.

docs.title: On the adapter card
docs.text:
MOTOR PWR XT30 socket on the mainboard; the adapter's plug is the mirror

The adapter card receives the bus on its own XT30 and distributes it:

  • Onefinity Redline and Elite: into pin 5 of each motor connector, since those machines carry motor power in the same cable as the signals.
  • AltMill: to five 2-pin 3.81 mm pluggable terminals, one per axis, matching the SLB-EXT arrangement.
  • DIY: to a pair of screw terminals.

The adapter's copper carries the full motor current, so those boards use wide pours rather than tracks.

docs.title: Power Supply
docs.text: ncCore runs from a single DC supply of 24 to 48 V. The same supply feeds the motors through the motor bus and every rail on the board.

docs.title: Choosing a supply
docs.text:
Machine Typical Notes Onefinity Elite 36 V The machine's own supply, up to about 13 A Onefinity Redline 36 or 48 V The machine's own supply AltMill 48 V, 12.5 A The machine's own supply DIY 24 to 48 V Size for the motors: add each driver's peak current, then 20 percent

The board's own consumption is small. What matters is the motor bus, which is limited on the board at about 18 A and fused at 5 A on the input. If your motors need more than 5 A in total from the supply, the input fuse will blow; see below.

Input fuse

F1 is a 5 A fuse in a holder. It protects the board's copper and the supply against a fault on the board. A build with four or five closed-loop motors on a hard run can exceed 5 A from the supply at 36 V. That is expected to change on production hardware; check the specification of your board revision before you assume the 5 A limit.

docs.title: Input connector
docs.text:
PWR IN, Mini-Fit Jr 2×3, header face. Three pins each side

J1 is a Mini-Fit Jr 2×3, the same pinout as the Onefinity Redline's PSU plug: three pins on one side are +, the three on the other are −. Use all three pins per side. A single pin is not rated for the motor current.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
• Reverse polarity: an ideal-diode controller with a MOSFET ahead of everything. A backwards supply lights the red REVERSED LED and nothing else happens.
  • Transient: a 58 V TVS on the input, rated for the 100 V front end.
  • Over-voltage lockout: the motor bus refuses to switch on above about 57 V, so a wrong or runaway supply never reaches the drivers.
  • Regeneration: decelerating steppers push energy back into the supply. The 100 V rating of the input stage and the TVS absorb normal excursions. A supply with no output capacitance and a machine with heavy rapids may still trip the OVLO; if that happens, add a bulk capacitor at the supply or a brake resistor module.

docs.title: Rails
docs.text: Rail Made by Feeds 24 V 100 V buck from the input Sensor supplies, aux outputs, the lower rails, the E-stop lamp 12 V Buck from 24 V Sensor supplies, the control-input wetting current 5 V Buck from 24 V, 3 A Sensor supplies, the line drivers, the E-stop loop, the fused 5V_X on the header 3.3 V LDO Field-side logic 5 V and 3.3 V logic Isolated DC-DC from the field 5 V MCU, radio, USB

docs.title: USB keep-alive
docs.text:
Either USB-C port's 5 V also feeds the logic side through a Schottky diode. If the machine's supply is cut, for example by an Onefinity E-stop at the PSU, the controller stays up on USB power, ncSender keeps its connection, and the board reports the stop instead of vanishing. It also means both chips can be flashed from a USB cable alone, with no machine power at all.

While on USB alone, the firmware treats the machine as unpowered: the bus-OK input is low, so homing is required before any motion once power returns.

docs.title: Emergency Stop
docs.text: ncCore's E-stop is a hardware chain. Firmware is not in the path. When the loop opens, motor power and the spindle enable are removed by circuits on the board, and the controller then reports what happened.

docs.title: How the chain works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[5 V through a PTC] --> B["OUT (pin 7)"]
  B --> C{"Mushroom (NC)<br/>door switches in series<br/>or the BYPASS jumper"}
  C --> D["RET (pin 6)"]
  D --> E[Motor-bus switch<br/>LM5069 enable]
  D --> F[Spindle isolator<br/>field-side supply]
  D --> G[MCU input<br/>ESTOP_S]
  E --> H[Motors]
  F --> I[Spindle PWM / EN / DIR]

The loop is a 5 V signal that leaves the board on OUT of the panel terminal, passes through your E-stop button's normally-closed contact, and comes back on RET. That returned signal is what enables the motor-bus switch and powers the field side of the spindle isolator.

What happens when the loop opens:

Element Effect How fast Motor bus The LM5069 hot-swap controller drops its output. Motor power is gone. Microseconds Spindle PWM, enable, direction The isolator's field side loses power, so all three lines go inactive. Microseconds Spindle 0–10 V Follows the PWM, so it falls to 0 V. Milliseconds (RC filter) Firmware The MCU sees ESTOP_S go inactive and raises a grblHAL alarm. Milliseconds

The mushroom head itself is the latch. Twisting it to release closes the loop again, but nothing restarts on its own: the motor bus soft-starts after about 80 ms of debounce, and grblHAL still needs an unlock and a soft reset before any motion. That is deliberate.

docs.title: Wiring the E-stop loop
docs.text:
The loop is on the seven-position panel terminal J44. See E-Stop Panel & Door for the full pinout.

  • Use the normally-closed contact of the mushroom button.
  • Add enclosure door switches or a second mushroom in series with the button. Any open contact anywhere in the loop stops the machine.
  • Keep the loop wiring short and away from motor and VFD cables. It carries 5 V through a PTC fuse.
  • A cut wire, a pulled plug or a dead loop supply all read as an open loop. The chain fails open.

The BYPASS jumper

J36, labelled E-STOP BYPASS, shorts OUT to RET on the board. It exists for machines whose E-stop cuts the DC supply upstream instead, such as the Onefinity Elite and Redline. With the jumper fitted there is no E-stop function on ncCore. Fit it only when your machine has its own E-stop that removes power, and never as a way to get a machine running.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Two things watch the chain:

  • ESTOP_S tells the firmware whether the loop is closed. grblHAL alarms when it opens.
  • MBUS_OK tells the firmware whether the motor bus is actually live. A power FET can fail shorted. If the loop is open but the bus is still live, the firmware must refuse to run and raise an alarm.

The green ENABLED LED next to the panel terminal is lit while the loop is closed.

docs.title: Restart procedure
docs.text:
1. Fix whatever caused the stop.
  2. Release the mushroom head.
  3. In ncSender, unlock the alarm and reset.
  4. Home the machine.

docs.title: Machines with their own E-stop
docs.text: Onefinity Elite and Redline controllers cut the 36 or 48 V supply at the PSU box when the mushroom is pressed. On those machines the whole board loses its input, but the logic side stays alive on USB power, so ncSender keeps its connection and reports the E-stop. Fit the BYPASS jumper and rely on the machine's own stop. See Power Supply for the USB keep-alive.

docs.title: General Safety
docs.text: A CNC router is a machine that moves heavy carriages at speed and spins a cutter at tens of thousands of rpm. The controller is one part of a system that includes your power supply, your motors, your spindle and your wiring. Read this page before you connect anything.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
• Work with the power supply off and unplugged when connecting or disconnecting anything on the board. The motor bus can carry up to 48 V at high current.
  • Never hot-plug the adapter header or the XT30. The ribbon carries signals only, but the XT30 carries the motor bus.
  • Check polarity before the first power-up. ncCore has an ideal-diode reverse-polarity protector on its input and a red REVERSED LED that lights if the supply is backwards. The board will not be damaged, but nothing will run until the wiring is corrected.
  • Fuse the input. The board has a user-replaceable 5 A fuse in a holder. Do not bypass it or fit a larger one.
  • Keep the field and logic grounds separate unless you understand why they are isolated.

docs.title: Mechanical
docs.text:
• Before the first move, confirm every axis direction in the air with the tool removed and low feed rates.
  • Home the machine after any power loss. The firmware requires it, and ncSender will prompt you.
  • Never rely on software alone to stop a machine. The E-stop is a hardware chain for that reason.

docs.title: Spindle and VFD
docs.text:
• A VFD can restart a spindle on its own when its run signal is asserted at power-up. ncCore removes the spindle enable in hardware when the E-stop loop opens, but you should still configure the VFD to require a fresh run command after a fault.
  • Route VFD power cables away from the sensor and signal wiring, and use shielded motor cable to the spindle.

docs.title: What ncCore is not
docs.text: ncCore is a hobby and prosumer machine controller. It has not been certified to any machinery safety standard. The E-stop chain is designed to fail safe, but it is your responsibility to assess the risks of your machine, add guarding and additional stops where you need them, and never leave a running machine unattended.

docs.title: Isolation & Grounding
docs.text:
ncCore has two electrical domains that never share a ground.

Domain Ground name What lives there Field GND Power input, motor bus, the 24 V, 12 V and 5 V rails, every machine input and output, the spindle circuits, the adapter header Logic DGND The STM32 MCU, the ESP32-S3 radio, both USB-C ports, the antenna

Every signal that crosses between them goes through an isolator: an optocoupler, a digital isolator, the isolated RS-485 transceiver, or the differential line drivers that need no ground reference at all. The logic side is powered through an isolated DC-DC converter.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A CNC machine is an electrically hostile place. A VFD switching kilowatts, a shorted 24 V sensor, or a ground loop through a long motor cable can put volts between "grounds" that should be the same. Isolation means none of that can reach the processor, the radio, or the USB port of your computer. It also means a fault on the machine side is far less likely to take the controller with it.

docs.title: What this means for your wiring
docs.text:
• Machine-side wiring returns to GND, the field ground. Sensor grounds, the VFD's common, the E-stop loop and the motor cables all belong there.
  • USB is on the logic side. Your PC's ground connects to DGND through the USB cable, and nowhere else. Nothing you wire to the machine terminals touches it.
  • Do not bridge GND and DGND. There is no star point on the board, on purpose. Bridging them defeats the isolation.
  • Chassis earth. Bond your machine frame, the spindle body and the VFD's earth terminal to protective earth per the VFD's manual. The board's four M3 mounting holes are isolated from both grounds, so mounting it on a grounded plate does not create a path.

docs.title: Static
docs.text: Handle the board by its edges. The MCU and radio are on the logic side and are protected by the isolation from machine-side events, but not from a static discharge straight into a USB connector or an exposed pin. Ground yourself before touching the board.
